binders: A sample type Ω equipped with a measurable-space structure.
A probability measure μ on Ω.
A family X indexed by ι of real-valued functions on Ω.
A family of real coefficients a indexed by ι.
hypotheses: Each function X i is Borel measurable.
The indexed family of functions X is mutually independent with respect to μ.
For every index i, the pushforward distribution of X i under μ is the fair symmetric two-point distribution assigning probability 1/2 to 1 and probability 1/2 to -1.
conclusions: The probability that the finite weighted sum ∑ i, a i X i is at least t is at most exp(-t^2 / (2 ∑ i, (a i)^2)).
mathematical_definitions: The prescribed common marginal law is obtained by taking a fair Bernoulli Boolean variable and mapping true to 1 and false to -1; equivalently, it is the Rademacher law with equal masses at -1 and 1.
The weighted random sum is S(ω) = ∑_{i∈ι} a_i X_i(ω), where the sum ranges over the entire finite index type.
The upper-tail event is {ω ∈ Ω | S(ω) >= t}.
The denominator uses the coefficient square sum ∑_{i∈ι} a_i^2.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For any finite family of independent measurable real random variables, each having the fair symmetric sign distribution on {-1,1}, any real coefficients a_i, and any nonnegative real t, the upper-tail probability of their weighted sum satisfies P(∑_i a_i X_i >= t) <= exp(-t^2/(2∑_i a_i^2)).

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The index type must be finite, but it need not be nonempty.
All random variables must have exactly the same fair two-point law supported on -1 and 1; the proposition does not cover general bounded, centered, or merely subgaussian variables.
The conclusion is one-sided and only assumes thresholds t >= 0.
The coefficients are arbitrary real numbers; no nonzero-coefficient hypothesis is present.

If the index type is empty or every coefficient is zero, then ∑ a_i^2 = 0. Real division in Lean is totalized, so the exponent evaluates using division by zero rather than requiring a positive denominator; in this case the right side is exp(0)=1.
The probability is expressed via Measure.real, the real conversion of the measure value. The probability-measure hypothesis makes the relevant measure finite, so no infinity-loss issue arises here.
Measurability and independence are separate explicit assumptions; the exact marginal-law equalities alone do not encode them.
The proposition does not explicitly assert centering or unit magnitude, although both follow from the prescribed marginal law.
